question: In its communication of 15 January 2026, Frontex states that irregular border crossings at the EU’s external borders fell by 26 % in total last year, while crossings at the eastern border with Belarus fell by a whopping 37 % to 10 846 ‘irregular border crossings’1.

However, the Polish Border Guard Headquarters reports that over 29 600 attempts to cross the Polish-Belarusian border were recorded between 1 January and 29 December 2025, nearly triple the figure that Frontex attributed to the entire region. Over 30 400 irregular border crossings were attempted the previous year, meaning that there has been a decrease of around 2.6 % between 2024 and 20252.

Data from our partners in Lithuanian and Latvia show record numbers, whether in terms of daily crossings or secondary migration movements, which have doubled according to Lithuanian data on the country’s border with Latvia3. During the LIBE meeting on 27 January 2026, Lithuania’s Minister of the Interior Vladislav Kondratovič mentioned a 20 % increase in crossings at the Lithuanian-Belarusian border.
Unfortunately, a Commission representative was unable to explain these radical divergences, both in terms of absolute values and trends. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the situation at the EU-Belarus border?

Does the Commission believe that migratory pressure has significantly reduced, in line with the data provided by Frontex, or are we seeing a continued attack at the same or an even higher rate than last year’s crisis level, in line with the information provided by countries bordering Belarus?
Is Frontex’s communication not misleading for the public?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.4.2026) In 2025, there were around 11 000 illegal border crossings (IBCs) at the EU’s eastern border1, according to consolidated Frontex data (–36% compared to 2024). At the EU’s external border with Belarus, the authorities of Poland, Latvia and Lithuania reported that, in 2025, there was again a high number of attempts to illegally cross the border.

This demonstrates that the weaponisation of migration continues at the EU’s external borders with Belarus. The difference between the data reported by Frontex and by the Member States is that Frontex uses a single definition of attempted IBCs applicable across the EU, while individual Member States collect data based on their own national definition of attempted IBCs.

There is currently no commonly agreed EU-wide definition for attempts to cross the border illegally. However, as part of the implementation of the Pact on Migration and Asylum, Frontex is working together with the Commission and Member States to establish an EU-wide common data collection on verifiable attempts to cross the border illegally. The Commission therefore does not consider the Frontex data misleading.
1 At the EU external borders with Russia, Belarus, Ukraine and Moldova.
